notes: Long-running Bank of Scotland guarantee enforcement; abuse of process and s24 Limitation Act issues are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Second action on judgment debt and abuse of process
key_facts: The Bank of Scotland lent to Galloway Seafood Co Ltd through Mr Bennett's guarantee and obtained a default judgment against him in 1995 but did not enforce it within six years.
After prolonged possession proceedings against Mrs Bennett failed in the House of Lords, the Bank issued a second action in May 2001 based on the 1995 judgment to preserve bankruptcy options.
Mr Bennett applied to strike out the second action as an abuse of process, arguing the Bank sought to circumvent the six-year bar on enforcing the first judgment.
Patten J refused strike-out and set aside a default judgment in the second action because interest exceeded six years under section 24(2).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Patten J's refusal to strike out the Bank's second action as an abuse of process.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; commencing a second action within six years to preserve bankruptcy rights was not an abuse of process even if Re A Debtor was later doubted.
enrichment.ratio: Bringing a second action on an existing judgment within the six-year period under section 24(1) of the Limitation Act 1980 is a matter of right and not per se an abuse of process; a judgment creditor may pursue such proceedings to preserve insolvency options where limitation on the original judgment is about to expire, provided there is a legitimate purpose and no culpable delay.
legal_issues: Whether a second action on a judgment debt is an abuse of process
Effect of section 24 on bankruptcy proceedings based on an earlier judgment
Whether the Bank had a legitimate purpose in issuing fresh proceedings
Impact of Ridgeway Motors on the common ground at first instance

notes: Detailed statutory construction of pension carry-forward under ICTA 1988; both tax and section 54 TMA issues are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Pension relief carry-forward for dual retirement annuity and personal pension contributors
key_facts: Ms Lonsdale, a barrister, contributed to both a pre-1988 retirement annuity contract and a post-1988 personal pension scheme.
She appealed General Commissioners' decisions on how unused relief from earlier years interacts with section 655 transitional provisions when both types of contribution are paid.
The Revenue contended unused relief must be aggregated and reduced by personal pension contributions paid in the current year.
Ms Lonsdale argued each year's unused relief should be kept separate and that a 1994/95 agreement with the Revenue bound future years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the General Commissioners for Income Tax.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on both questions; the Revenue's construction of sections 625 and 655(1)(b) was preferred and no binding section 54 agreement was found.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 655(1)(b) of ICTA 1988, relief carried forward under section 625 by reference to unused relief for any year must be calculated using all accrued unused relief available at that year of assessment, reduced by personal pension contributions paid in the same year; a section 54 agreement fixing liability for one year cannot bind the Revenue as to carry-forward amounts in later years.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'unused relief for any year' in section 655(1)(b)
Whether earlier years' unused relief is aggregated before reduction by personal pension contributions
Whether a section 54 agreement over 1994/95 figures bound the Revenue for subsequent years
Interaction of sections 619, 625, 639, 642 and 655

Tod (H.M.I.T) v South Essex Motors (Basildon) Ltd (1987) 60 TC 598
McNiven (H.M.I.T.) v Westmoreland Investments Ltd (1997) 73 TC 1

notes: Crisis interim relief JR on residential placement; balance of convenience and precautionary approach clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Interim placement for severely epileptic adult leaving college
key_facts: The 22-year-old claimant has severe epilepsy with risk of sudden unexpected death, moderate to severe learning difficulties, and was leaving St Piers college imminently.
Sutton LBC proposed interim placement at Regard Partnership's Grove; the claimant preferred Independence Homes, a specialist epilepsy provider.
Independence Homes was available at about £1,400 per week versus £1,233 at the Grove, with disputed adequacy of epilepsy training at the Grove.
The local authority delayed finalising placement until immediately before the hearing, leaving inadequate evidence on epilepsy care at the Grove.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Oral hearing for interim relief pending permission to apply for judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Interim relief granted; on balance of convenience and a precautionary approach, the claimant should go to Independence Homes pending substantive resolution.
enrichment.ratio: Where interim residential placement turns on serious epilepsy risk and the local authority has failed to adduce adequate evidence that a non-specialist proposed home can manage seizures, the court may prefer the specialist provider on the balance of convenience even if slightly more expensive and even if that may influence the substantive dispute.
legal_issues: Whether interim relief should require placement at Independence Homes or Regard Partnership
Application of balance of convenience and serious issue to be tried
Whether Article 8 requires a precautionary approach to epilepsy risk
Relevance of cost difference for interim relief

notes: Complex excise fraud winding-up rescission application; discretion analysis and withdrawal of opposition are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Rescission of winding-up order over disputed excise duty assessments

statutes_considered.title: Excise Duty Points (Duty Suspended Movements of Excise Goods) Regulations 2001

key_facts: Turnstem Ltd traded alcohol in bond; Customs assessed about £2.7m VAT and excise duty on 27 consignments allegedly diverted from bonded warehouses.
A provisional liquidator was appointed, Tribunal appeals were withdrawn, and Turnstem submitted to a compulsory winding-up order on 13 January 2004.
Mr Bhanderi applied to rescind the order relying on fresh evidence, a pending third Tribunal appeal, and the decision in Jack Baars Wholesale.
Lawrence Collins J found opposition had been withdrawn tactically and that Turnstem was insolvent even apart from the petition debt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under Insolvency Rules 1986 rule 7.47 to rescind a compulsory winding-up order made on an unopposed petition.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; no change of circumstances or fresh evidence justified rescission and the withdrawal of opposition was not based on misunderstanding.
enrichment.ratio: The court will rarely rescind a winding-up order except on changed circumstances or newly discovered evidence unavailable on appeal; a genuinely disputed excise assessment should ordinarily be resolved in the VAT and Duties Tribunal rather than on a winding-up petition, but tactical withdrawal of opposition followed by a rescission application will not succeed where the company is insolvent and the applicant knew of pending Tribunal proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether rescission was justified by the Baars decision or undisclosed Tribunal appeal
Effect of tachograph evidence on the existence of the petition debt
Propriety of provisional liquidator withdrawing company appeals
Validity of DSMEG Regulation 7(2) and disputed duty assessments

notes: Re-trial on Holme v Brunskill discharge of football club guarantor; factual findings on September 1994 meeting are extensive and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Guarantor discharge after variation of football club bank facility
key_facts: Mr Hayward gave three all-monies guarantees totalling up to £650,000 to Lloyds TSB for Bournemouth & Boscombe Athletic Football Club.
On 23 September 1994 the Bank and Club agreed a facility letter restructuring debt, with Ken Gardiner providing a £250,000 collateral-backed guarantee.
Hayward sold most of his shares and understood Gardiner's guarantee would cover missed 1996/97 repayments without triggering default until June 1997.
The Club failed to pay the June 1996 instalment; Gardiner's guarantee was called and a subsequent side letter required replacement security for the second year.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Re-trial ordered by the Court of Appeal on what was agreed at the 23 September 1994 meeting and whether subsequent variation discharged the guarantor.
enrichment.outcome: Bank's claim fails; Mr Hayward's guarantees were discharged under Holme v Brunskill before demand because the Club and Bank varied the facility without his consent.
enrichment.ratio: Where a creditor and principal debtor agree after the guarantee is given to a variation that materially prejudices the guarantor without his consent, the rule in Holme v Brunskill discharges the guarantor; an oral agreement that recourse to a third-party guarantee would not constitute default until the next repayment date can coexist with a later side letter varying terms to the guarantor's detriment.
legal_issues: What was agreed at the 23 September 1994 meeting about Gardiner's guarantee
Whether failure to pay the June 1996 instalment was an event of default
Effect of the Gardiner side letter as a subsequent variation
Application of Holme v Brunskill and exclusion clauses in standard bank guarantees
linked_authorities: Holme v Brunskill (1877) 3 QBD 495
Lloyds TSB Bank Plc v Hayward [earlier CA order 12 December 2002]

notes: Short criminal appeal on Sex Offenders Act notification after conditional discharge; statutory interaction clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Sex offender notification requirements after conditional discharge
key_facts: Gary Dean Longworth pleaded guilty to two counts of making indecent photographs of children and received concurrent 12-month conditional discharges.
Indecent images at level 1 were found on his computer after he took it for repair; adult pornography was not charged.
The sentencing judge ruled that Part I Sex Offenders Act 1997 notification requirements still applied despite the conditional discharge.
Conflicting earlier cases included Malone [2001] 2 Cr App R (S) 43 and Oliver [2003] 2 Cr App R (S) 15.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence with leave, challenging whether notification requirements apply after conditional discharge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; notification requirements under the 1997 Act apply and the conviction remains a conviction for that purpose under section 14(1) of the 2000 Act.
enrichment.ratio: Notification requirements under the Sex Offenders Act 1997 are ancillary to criminal proceedings and fall within the exception in section 14(1) of the Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000, so a conditional discharge does not prevent the offender being a 'person of any other description' subject to five years' notification from conviction.
legal_issues: Whether a conditional discharge means the conviction is not a conviction for Sex Offenders Act purposes
Interaction of section 14(1) and section 14(3) of the 2000 Act
Whether notification is a disqualification or disability under section 14(3)
Reconciliation of Malone and Oliver
linked_authorities: Malone [2001] 2 Cr App R (S) 43
Oliver [2003] 2 Cr App R (S) 15
Ibbotson v United Kingdom [1999] Crim LR 153

enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal unfair redundancy dismissal refused
key_facts: Mr Learnihan, a senior analyst/programmer at TDK UK Ltd, was dismissed for redundancy in August 2002 while on sick leave.
The three-person IT pool was reduced after workload fell; the IT manager could absorb the claimant's duties.
The Employment Tribunal found redundancy a fair reason but no consultation had occurred; it held consultation would have been pointless.
Burton J dismissed the EAT Rule 3(10) application for lack of error of law.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal and extension of time against EAT dismissal of unfair dismissal appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused and extension of time not needed; no real prospect of success on any asserted error of law.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to consult before redundancy can render dismissal unfair but not where the tribunal finds as a fact that consultation would have served no practical purpose; challenges to selection criteria and alternative employment are findings of fact not appealable as errors of law.
legal_issues: Whether lack of consultation rendered dismissal unfair
Whether selection criteria drafted by a redundant candidate were unfair
Failure to consider alternative employment within the organisation
Whether EAT erred in law under Rule 3(10)

notes: Asylum appeal on Sinhalese interpretation quality; adjudicator's note supports dismissal though late solicitor statement noted.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal alleging inadequate Sinhalese interpretation
key_facts: Mr Perera, a Sri Lankan asylum seeker, claimed risk from a UNP minister because of his family's JVP involvement.
The adjudicator rejected his credibility, citing inconsistencies and delay in claiming asylum; his brother succeeded in separate proceedings.
The solicitor challenged the Sinhalese interpreter before and during the hearing; the adjudicator checked with the interpreter manager at lunch.
The Court of Appeal had the adjudicator's sixteen-page hearing note, not before the IAT, and analysed a alleged misunderstanding about which party was in power 1993–2001.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission granted by Mummery and Pill LJJ against IAT dismissal of asylum and human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; interpretation was adequate and adverse credibility findings did not depend on the disputed oral evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Where an adjudicator enquires about an interpreter, offers involvement of the interpreter manager, and contemporaneously records proceedings, a general complaint without specific failures will not vitiate findings especially where core adverse findings rest on documentary inconsistencies; a momentary misunderstanding corrected in cross-examination does not show the adjudicator lacked understanding of Sri Lankan political history.
legal_issues: Whether inadequate Sinhalese interpretation denied a fair hearing
Adjudicator's duty when interpretation is challenged
Whether misunderstanding about UNP being in power affected credibility findings
Whether failure to align with brother's successful appeal was an error of law

confidence.notes: Outcome and interpretation analysis are clear. A late solicitor statement was admitted but did not alter the result.

enrichment.short_title: Armed forces pension credit member must wait until age 60
key_facts: Lady Smith received half her ex-husband's Armed Forces Pension Scheme rights under a 2003 pension sharing order when she was 56 and he was 59 and already in receipt of pension.
Statutory normal benefit age for pension credit members of occupational schemes is 60–65; AFPS pays credit members from age 60, creating an interim income gap.
She sought a declaration that sections 101B and 101C of the Pension Schemes Act 1993 were incompatible with Articles 1P, 8 and 14 of the ECHR.
Wilson J held indirect sex discrimination was justified and the impugned provision did not interfere with her convention rights as alleged.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for declaration of incompatibility under section 4(2) Human Rights Act 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no declaration of incompatibility; claimant ordered to pay defendants' costs; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Preventing payment of pension credit benefits from an unfunded occupational scheme until normal benefit age (60 for AFPS) encourages work until retirement age and yields a higher later pension; indirect discrimination against ex-wives where the active member draws pension before 60 is objectively justified and does not breach Articles 1P, 8 or 14 because pension credit rights are defined by Parliament rather than unlawfully withheld possessions.
legal_issues: Whether deferring pension credit payments until age 60 breaches Article 1 Protocol 1
Whether the income gap infringes Article 8 private life
Indirect discrimination against women and divorced ex-wives under Article 14
Whether sections 101C(2) regulations could provide a lawful remedy

notes: Parallel import trade mark case applying Davidoff consent principles; liability findings are detailed and clear.

enrichment.short_title: Quiksilver parallel imports sold without proprietor's consent
key_facts: Palimar manufactured genuine Quiksilver goods under a licence limited to Asian territories and sold a consignment intended for Sovincom in the former Soviet republics.
Financier MFC took security; after Sovincom defaulted MFC sold the goods through wholesalers to Trago Mills in Cornwall.
The defendant sold the goods believing they had been lawfully put on the EEA market; Quiksilver and exclusive licensee Na Pali sued for infringement.
The court found Palimar never unequivocally consented to EEA marketing and Quiksilver was not bound by any implied Palimar consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on liability only; quantum of damages reserved for enquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Trade mark infringement established; Quiksilver did not consent under section 12; Na Pali had standing as exclusive licensee to sue.
enrichment.ratio: Consent to place trade-marked goods on the EEA market must unequivocally demonstrate renunciation of exclusive rights; it cannot be inferred from silence, unrestricted resale clauses, or a financier's ability to resell after default; a territorial licensee without authority to consent for the proprietor cannot bind the trade mark owner, and failure to sue an intermediary does not imply consent.
legal_issues: Whether Palimar consented to EEA marketing within section 12(1)
Whether Palimar's consent bound Quiksilver as proprietor
Whether Quiksilver impliedly consented by monitoring or not suing MFC
Whether Na Pali as exclusive licensee had locus standi
